name: Rendsburg
title: Rendsburg Ship Gauging: UTM on the Kiel Canal
description: Ship gauging in Rendsburg on the Kiel Canal: UTM for heavy-lift ships, coasters, feeders and small tankers, covering decks, holds, tanks and piping.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging for Canal Traffic and Heavy-Lift Ships at Rendsburg
intro: Rendsburg sits halfway along the Kiel Canal, where thousands of transits a year pass the town and its heavy-cargo terminal on the south bank. Most ships do not stop, but those loading project cargo, waiting for a berth or making a planned halt in the canal give a superintendent a few hours with the ship tied up and steady. We use that time for targeted thickness gauging. The technicians fly in from India for each assignment and join the vessel at the quay the agent has arranged.

highlights.p: Multipurpose and heavy-lift ships loading at the canal-side terminal carry concentrated loads on tank tops and tween decks. While cranes are rigged and cargo is secured, the team can gauge those decks and check the welds left behind where sea-fastenings were cut away.

highlights.h: Gauging while the canal passes by
highlights.p: Feeders, coasters and small tankers on the North Sea to Baltic route sometimes halt at Rendsburg for stores, crew or a cargo delay. A pre-agreed list of tanks, pipe runs or deck areas can be measured before the ship rejoins the transit.

highlights.h: Riding the transit, lock to lock
highlights.p: Where the master agrees, technicians can board at one end of the canal and leave at the other, gauging engine-room piping and tanks already certified gas-free during the passage. Nothing changes in the ship's schedule, and the readings are ready on arrival.

port.h: Rendsburg: the midpoint of the Kiel Canal
p: The Kiel Canal crosses Schleswig-Holstein from Brunsbüttel on the Elbe estuary to Kiel-Holtenau on the Baltic, and Rendsburg lies near its middle, where the canal meets the old course of the River Eider. The town grew up around that crossing. Today the canal passes south of the historic centre, under the railway high bridge, and the Obereider lake joins it beside the town. Canal pilots change over at Rüsterbergen, a short distance to the west, so most ships pass Rendsburg with a fresh pilot on the bridge and the second half of the transit still ahead of them. Because the town is well away from both lock complexes, a stop here divides the passage neatly in two, and ships that need a break in the transit for stores, crew or a cargo appointment often take it at Rendsburg.

The traffic is a cross-section of North European short-sea shipping. Feeder container ships shuttle between Hamburg or Bremerhaven and Baltic ports, coasters carry grain, fertiliser, timber and steel, small product and chemical tankers run between refineries and coastal depots, and ro-ro and heavy-lift ships use the canal to avoid the longer route round Denmark. Yachts and naval ships from the canal's own shipyards also pass on their way to sea trials. Container feeders keep to tight weekly rotations, whereas tramp coasters may learn their next cargo only a day ahead, and that difference decides how much warning we get before a job. Ships of every flag share a narrow channel with strict speed rules and passing places, so a stop has to be arranged with the canal's traffic control through the agent rather than improvised.

Two kinds of port activity bring ships alongside at Rendsburg. The heavy-cargo terminal at Osterrönfeld, on the south bank, handles project cargo, large machinery and energy components that arrive by road and are lifted aboard multipurpose and heavy-lift ships. Because those components travel on special road convoys booked well in advance, the ship's time alongside is one of the more predictable windows anywhere on the canal. The older town harbour off the Obereider serves smaller ships with bulk and general cargo, handled for businesses in the town and the farming country around it. Severe winters can bring ice to the canal and the Obereider; it rarely stops traffic, but an ice-class ship heading for the northern Baltic may well pass Rendsburg in January on her way to harder conditions.

facilities.h: Where a ship can be gauged in and around Rendsburg
p: Rendsburg has no merchant drydock. The shipyards along this stretch of the canal build yachts and naval vessels, so a cargo ship needing a docking survey goes to a repair yard in Hamburg, on the North Sea coast or elsewhere on the Baltic. What Rendsburg offers is quay time. A heavy-lift ship may lie at the Osterrönfeld terminal while cargo is delivered, slung and secured, and with holds open and decks clear of the loading area, the team works through tank tops, tween decks, hatch covers and coamings.

In the town harbour, coasters loading or discharging bulk cargo give windows of a day or two, enough for hold, double-bottom and ballast tank readings once the crew has emptied and ventilated the spaces. A ship stopping at a canal berth for stores, crew or repairs is a smaller opportunity, and the scope is matched to the hours the canal authority has agreed. For anything larger than that, the readings taken here usually prepare the steel list for the docking yard.
list: Heavy-cargo terminal at Osterrönfeld — tank top, tween-deck and hatch-cover gauging on heavy-lift and multipurpose ships while project cargo is loaded.
Town harbour off the Obereider — hold, double-bottom and ballast tank readings on coasters during bulk and general cargo calls.
Canal berths arranged through the agent — short, pre-scoped stops for deck, piping or tank gauging on feeders and small tankers.
Riding squad between Brunsbüttel and Kiel-Holtenau — engine-room piping and gas-free tanks measured during the transit, with the master's agreement.
Docking yards elsewhere — Rendsburg readings handed to the yard and class surveyor so steel renewal is planned before the ship arrives.

context.h: Canal rules, port state control and the short-sea fleet
p: The Kiel Canal is a federal waterway run by the German waterways and shipping administration, with its own traffic rules, pilotage requirements and restrictions on certain dangerous cargoes. A ship entering it has to be fit to steer and manoeuvre in a narrow channel, so superintendents of older canal traders like to know the condition of steering gear compartments, sea water lines and hull structure before a transit rather than after. Ships berthed at Rendsburg fall under German port state control within the Paris MoU, carried out by the Ship Safety Division of BG Verkehr, and canal traffic includes many of the older, smaller ships that the Paris MoU targeting system flags for closer attention.

Many canal ships are below the size thresholds of the larger EU emissions rules, but owners still feel them. General cargo ships between 400 and 5,000 GT have had to monitor and report emissions under the EU MRV regulation since 2025, and ships calling at EU ports, whatever their flag, need an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. For an owner deciding whether an ageing coaster is worth another renewal survey, a set of thickness readings taken at a canal stop is often the first hard evidence on the table.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Rendsburg
jobs.p: Work at Rendsburg is short and opportunistic, built around a loading slot, a cargo delay or the canal transit itself. The superintendent usually sends the TM plan or the last survey report, flags the areas of concern and tells us how long the ship will be tied up. We then rank the spaces so the most important readings come first, and agree with the chief officer which tanks the crew will empty and ventilate ahead of arrival. Heavy-lift ships add crack detection to the list, because the fittings welded on and cut off for each voyage leave marks in the deck that need checking. Examples:
list: A heavy-lift ship loading a transformer at Osterrönfeld: tank-top and tween-deck gauging under the cargo footprint, with magnetic particle testing where sea-fastenings from the last voyage were removed.
A coaster discharging fertiliser in the town harbour: hold frames, lower brackets and tank-top plating gauged once the hold is swept, since corrosive residues attack bare steel quickly.
A feeder container ship stopping at a canal berth for a crew change: scrubber wash-water and overboard lines measured with the system shut down.
A product tanker transiting from the Elbe to the Baltic: engine-room sea water and fuel lines gauged by a riding team during the canal passage.
Pre-purchase gauging of a general cargo ship lying idle at a canal berth: holds, ballast tanks and hatch coamings measured for the buyer.

logistics: Hamburg Airport is the usual arrival point, with rail connections north through Neumünster to Rendsburg; Kiel and Brunsbüttel are within reach by road for jobs that start or finish at the locks. Germany is in the Schengen area, so the technicians need Schengen visas, and we plan around their lead time. The ship's agent arranges the canal stop with traffic control, the berth and any access to the heavy-cargo terminal, and for riding squads confirms with the master where the team boards and disembarks.
vessels: Coasters and short-sea general cargo ships
Yachts and naval ships on delivery from canal yards

faqs.q: Can thickness gauging be done during a Kiel Canal transit?
faqs.a: Yes, for spaces that can be entered safely while the ship is under way. A riding team boards at Brunsbüttel or Holtenau and measures engine-room piping, steering gear compartment structure and tanks that are already gas-free during the passage. Enclosed-space entry follows the ship's permit system, and the master decides what is allowed. Holds and ballast tanks needing ventilation are better left for a planned stop alongside.

faqs.q: Can a heavy-lift ship be gauged while it loads at Osterrönfeld?
faqs.a: Usually, if the work is kept away from the lifting zone. While cargo is being delivered and slung, the team gauges holds, tank tops and decks not in use, and moves to the loaded areas only when the crane work there is finished. Where sea-fastenings from an earlier voyage were cut off, the deck is checked for thinning and cracks before new fittings are welded on.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock at Rendsburg?
faqs.a: Not for merchant ships. The shipyards near Rendsburg build yachts and naval vessels, so cargo ships due for a docking go to repair yards in Hamburg, on the North Sea coast or elsewhere on the Baltic. Gauging at Rendsburg is done afloat, and the readings, tied to frame and strake references, help the docking yard and the class surveyor plan steel renewal before the ship arrives.

faqs.q: How long does a ship need to stop at Rendsburg for gauging?
faqs.a: It depends on the scope rather than the place. A few pipe runs or a deck area can be measured in a stop of a few hours. A set of ballast tanks needs time for the crew to empty, ventilate and gas-test them first, so it fits a cargo call of a day or more. We size the scope to the time the agent has agreed with the canal authority.

faqs.q: Does winter ice in the canal affect gauging work?
faqs.a: Rarely in practice. Ice in the canal is occasional and seldom halts traffic, but cold weather affects deck work, couplant and coatings, so exposed readings take longer. Ice-class ships heading for the northern Baltic often pass Rendsburg in midwinter, and owners sometimes use a stop here to check ice-belt framing from inside the wing tanks before the ship reaches the ice.
